claim_text: Radiolarian and similar siliceous skeletons approximate geodesic/minimal frameworks on a sphere (latticed shells as systems of shortest lines and near-equal partitions).

state_variables.V: set of junction vertices on the shell
state_variables.E: set of strut edges between junctions
state_variables.L_e: length of edge e (geodesic / great-circle arc length on S^2)
state_variables.valence(v): number of edges incident at vertex v

boundary_conditions: Shell approximates a closed spherical surface (Thompson treats radiolarian tests as spherical lattices).
Struts follow shortest paths on the sphere (great circles) rather than arbitrary Euclidean chords in R^3 when projected.
Partitions of the surface into near-equal cells (Thompson: 'near-equal partitions').

equations.name: Great-circle geodesic length
equations.formula: L_g(p,q) = R * arccos(p . q)  for unit directions p, q on S^2
equations.role: Shortest curve between two points on the sphere

equations.name: Equal partition on equator
equations.formula: n equal azimuthal arcs of length 2 pi R / n have identical geodesic length

equations.name: Icosahedral geodesic refinement
equations.formula: Subdivide icosahedron faces, project to S^2; edges are great-circle segments
equations.role: Reference minimal framework used for morphometric comparison

empirical_claims: Haeckel/Challenger radiolarian tests show polygonal lattices suggestive of geodesic nets.
Thompson compares such shells to systems of shortest lines on a sphere.
